speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill also contains two other sets of amendments not related to the Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Bill – one set led by the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) and the other by the Ministry of Finance (MOF).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will explain the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), MinLaw and MOF's amendments in my opening speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will address questions pertaining to the amendments led by MHA and MinLaw.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Second Minister for Finance, Ms Indranee Rajah, will address questions pertaining to MOF's amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Illicit drug supply, drug abuse and the potency of some narcotic drugs are reaching unprecedented levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The 2022 World Drug Report published by the UN Office of Drugs and Crime (UNODC) found that young people abuse drugs more than adults.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The UNODC also found that, in many countries, the levels of drug abuse among the youth have reached record levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The number of deaths worldwide associated with drug abuse increased by 17.5% between 2009 and 2019, reaching about half a million deaths in 2019.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Drugs cause great harm to individuals, families and the society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Many countries around the world have given up on this fight, because drug trafficking and use have become so prevalent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For these countries, the only practical approach is to reduce the harm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Our tough laws have kept the drug situation here relatively under control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We must continue to keep drugs at bay, to prevent the harms from overwhelming us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Over the last few years, we have seen the rise of a new threat in the drug landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: New psychoactive substances, or NPS for short, are synthetically-produced substances which mimic the effects of traditional controlled drugs, such as cocaine, heroin and cannabis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: NPS are harmful and their abuse has been linked to adverse physical and psychological reactions and also overdose deaths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These substances are no less harmful than controlled drugs and are similar in effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The UNODC has reported that NPS users are frequently hospitalised with severe intoxication.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In Singapore, there have been at least four NPS-related deaths since 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Because the psychoactive effect that NPS causes is similar to that of a controlled drug, its abuse will also lead to acts of crime and violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Members will remember some recent cases within Singapore where drug abusers acted violently, such as the lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) abuser, who killed his mother and grandmother in 2019; or the methamphetamine abuser, who attacked two other diners with a knife in a restaurant in 2022 because his food was not ready.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have not seen similar incidents arising from NPS abuse yet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We should nip the NPS problem in the bud.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Currently, we manage NPS in the following way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Once we detect an NPS, we will list its molecular structure in the Fifth Schedule of Misuse of Drugs Act, or MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Section 58A of the MDA allows for such listing up to a year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: During this one-year period, the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB), can seize the substance to prevent its proliferation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: CNB will use this time to conduct industry consultations to determine if the substance has any legitimate uses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: During this one year, CNB cannot take any prosecutorial action against a person trafficking in the substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If there are no legitimate uses, its molecular structure will subsequently be listed in the First Schedule of MDA as a controlled drug.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Only when it is listed in the First Schedule, can a person who is found trafficking, manufacturing, importing, exporting or possessing such NPS be prosecuted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The limitation of the current approach is that we will always be playing catch-up with the syndicates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The ease in modifying the molecular structure of NPS to create new variants means that traffickers can easily overcome our laws by switching to new, unlisted NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In fact, drug suppliers are known to tailor the molecular structure of NPS, according to what is not yet controlled through legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We need to put in place a more proactive approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We studied the drug legislation in the United Kingdom and Australia and adopted parts of them, to develop our own unique framework to tackle NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We are proposing a new legislative framework to deal with the NPS threat, based on their capacity to produce a psychoactive effect rather than their molecular structure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This allows CNB to take enforcement action against potentially dangerous and potent NPS, and not have to wait until their molecular structure has been identified and listed in MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The new framework criminalises the manufacture, import and export, traffic, possession and consumption of all psychoactive substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The first limb of the definition of a psychoactive substance, as inserted by clause 2, is a substance or product which is capable of producing a psychoactive effect if consumed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: NPS, in this Bill, will be referred to, generally, as "psychoactive substances". "Psychoactive effect" is defined to mean the stimulation or depression, whether directly or indirectly, of the individual's central nervous system, affecting the individual's mental functioning or emotional state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The new Fifth Schedule will list substances that have the capacity to have a psychoactive effect on an individual, but with legitimate uses; or those which are already regulated under other legislation, such as caffeine, alcohol, food, tobacco and any medicinal product.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I explained the method of temporary listing earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The existing Fifth Schedule used to temporarily list NPS will be repealed, since there is no longer a need for temporary listing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To be clear, there is no change to the existing regime for controlled drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: All controlled drugs listed in the First Schedule will continue to be regulated in the same way as before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: That is why controlled drugs are also listed as excluded substances in the new Fifth Schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The proposed definition of "psychoactive substances" covers a broad scope of substances with different levels of psychoactivity and, because they are novel, their potential harms may not be as well-documented as those of controlled drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This approach, therefore, balances the need for deterrence against the uncertainty over the universe of psychoactive substances, with varying levels of potential harm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This substance will, at that point, no longer be treated as a psychoactive substance, as defined in the MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In 2019, we introduced offences to criminalise acts of contamination that contribute to the spread of drug abuse and child endangerment through exposure to drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 7 introduces the same contamination and child endangerment offences for psychoactive substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The punishments will be the same as the offences, where Class C controlled drugs are involved, including caning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We propose for caning to be retained for contamination offences, to better protect vulnerable members of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Repeat offenders with antecedents of the same nature, whether for psychoactive substances or controlled drugs, will be liable for higher punishments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, if an offender has an antecedent for trafficking in a controlled drug and is now convicted of trafficking in a psychoactive substance, he will be considered a repeat offender and will be subject to enhanced punishment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will now speak about issues relating to the element of knowledge for offences concerning psychoactive substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The MDA currently contains statutory presumptions relating to controlled drugs which, when invoked, shift the burden of proof to the accused person to prove otherwise on a balance of probabilities, for example, that he did not have knowledge of the nature of the drug found in his possession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clauses 10 to 14 extend these presumptions to psychoactive substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: An accused person who claims that the psychoactive substance is an excluded substance, bears the burden of proving this claim on a balance of probabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For the new offences criminalising the manufacture, import and export, traffic and possession of psychoactive substances introduced in clause 7, it is a defence for the accused person to prove on a balance of probabilities that he dealt with the substance for a legitimate purpose, other than human consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The burden for proving this defence, likewise, falls on the accused person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, if a person is arrested with a substance found to be capable of producing a psychoactive effect and claims that he intended to use the substance as a cleaning chemical, he would need to produce evidence to show that he intended to use the psychoactive substance in his possession for cleaning, and not for human consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is fair, as there is a wide range of substances that have the capacity to have a psychoactive effect on a person if consumed, with an equally wide range of uses for these substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The person dealing in the substance would know best what the substance is and the intended use of the substance, if it truly has a legitimate purpose other than for abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In addition, clause 15 inserts a new section 22B, which provides that "knowledge that a substance is a psychoactive substance" is established, for the purposes of offences concerning psychoactive substances, if the person knew the substance had the capacity to have a psychoactive effect on an individual when consumed and did not know, or have reason to believe, that the substance is an excluded substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For avoidance of doubt, section 22B provides that the person need not have known the exact name or molecular structure of the substance, in order for his knowledge of the psychoactive substance to be established.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Scientific certificates issued under section 16 may be used as proof of the matters contained within, relating to controlled drugs, unless the contrary is proved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 9 extends the effect of section 16 to apply to certificates relating to psychoactive substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Operationally, the Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX), will be conducting the relevant tests on seized substances during investigations into an offence relating to psychoactive substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As such, clause 9 also amends section 16 to allow HTX analysts to sign certificates issued under section 16.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clauses 16, 17 and 18 extend officers' powers of search, seizure and arrest to apply in relation to psychoactive substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 19 amends section 27 to allow for the forfeiture of any psychoactive substance seized under the MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clauses 21, 22 and 23 amend sections 31, 31A and 31B to extend officers' powers to collect urine specimens, hair specimens and oral fluids in cases of suspected psychoactive substance abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Where appropriate, abusers of psychoactive substances may be subjected to treatment and rehabilitation, similar to abusers of controlled drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 2(b) expands the definition of "drug addict" to include a person who is addicted to a psychoactive substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This allows the Director of CNB to subject him to supervision, or treatment and rehabilitation, which includes committal to the Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will also amend Article 9(6)(b) of the Constitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Article 9(6)(b) ensures that laws relating to the misuse of drugs, such as the MDA, that authorise the arrest and detention of any person for the purpose of treatment and rehabilitation, are valid under the Constitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We propose to include psychoactive substances into this clause, to ensure the constitutional validity of the Director of CNB's proposed powers to commit persons who have abused psychoactive substances to detention for treatment and rehabilitation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Bill will make consequential and related amendments to nine other Acts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These are technical amendments needed to align these Acts with the new legislative framework for NPS, such as to update the enforcement powers in those Acts to also cover psychoactive substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will now move on to explain the second key amendment in the Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In recent years, CNB has seen the modus operandi of syndicates shift towards dealing in larger quantities of drugs per transaction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, in September 2022, there was a large seizure of 13 kilogrammes of drugs, which had included eight kilogrammes of cannabis, as well as a seizure of 18 kilogrammes of heroin in May 2022.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These were exceptionally large seizures, amounting to millions of dollars in street value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The current punishments for possession offences are not differentiated by the type of drugs involved and are not tiered based on the quantity of the drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It, therefore, does not sufficiently account for the greater harms that could be caused by a person in possession of larger quantities of drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Persons who are willing to risk being in possession of such large quantities of drugs contribute significantly to fuelling the local drug market and feeding local drug demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The drugs for which this amendment will apply are: cannabis, cannabis mixture, cannabis resin, cocaine, diamorphine, methamphetamine, morphine and opium.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We scoped the new framework to these eight drugs, based on our assessment that they have the highest potential to cause serious harms in our local context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Currently, the maximum punishment for possession of any controlled drug, regardless of weight, is 10 years' imprisonment or a fine of up to $20,000, or both.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Bill proposes to tier the penalties according to the quantity of the controlled drug.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In the proposed enhanced punishment framework, for the lowest tier, the punishment is a maximum of 10 years' imprisonment or a fine of up to $20,000, or both.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Since 2019, we have been diverting "pure" drug abusers to DRC for treatment and rehabilitation, instead of prosecuting them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Minister for Home Affairs had explained then that "pure" abusers referred to drug abusers who did not commit any other offences besides drug consumption, but who may face other less serious, related drug offences, such as possession of drug-taking utensils or small quantities of drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, drug abusers found with large amounts of drugs in their possession would not be considered "pure" drug abusers and would not be considered for diversion to the DRC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There is, thus, no change to the approach we take for "pure" drug abusers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Bill will also make some technical amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The current definition of "article liable to seizure" in section 2 includes any money, thing, controlled equipment, controlled material, or anything that contains evidence of an offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This may not apply intuitively to things that "constitute" and do not "contain" evidence of an offence, like jewellery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 2 amends the definition to include the word "constitute".

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This will align with the language used for a similar provision relating to seizure of evidence in the Criminal Procedure Code 2010, or CPC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Next, section 11 of the MDA makes it an offence for an owner, tenant, occupier or person-in-charge of any place or premises, to permit that place to be used for drug consumption or trafficking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 3 amends section 11 to clarify that such a person only commits an offence if the drug consumption mentioned in section 11(a) is in contravention of section 8(b) for being unauthorised, which constitutes the drug consumption offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Next, section 11C criminalises introducing a person whom he knows is a drug trafficker to another person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 5 amends section 11C to clarify that a person, A, only commits a section 11C offence if A knows or has reason to believe that B intends to procure a controlled drug and the possession of the controlled drug by B or any person B passes it to, would not be authorised under the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Likewise, person A would only be liable for the section 11C offence if he knows or has reason to believe that B intends, without any authorisation under the Act, to smoke, administer or consume the controlled drug.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To illustrate, if someone offers to introduce his friend to a person whom he knows is a drug trafficker, he will only be liable for a section 11C offence if he knows or believes that this friend intends to buy drugs from this trafficker for unauthorised consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will also make amendments to sections 24, 25 and 26 to clarify that an officer may make seizures based on reasonable suspicion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clauses 16, 17 and 18 make these amendments respectively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The current sections 24, 25 and 26, if read literally, seem to suggest that CNB can only seize any drug, substance or article which is confirmed to be a controlled drug or substance, article liable to seizure, drug specified in the Fifth Schedule or substance containing any drug specified in that Schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In practice, it is not possible for CNB to only seize such drugs, substances or articles after confirmation of their nature, since this can only be confirmed after the drug, substance or article has undergone scientific analysis, after seizure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Likewise, section 24 suggests that officers can only seize or detain any vehicle which has been confirmed to be used in the commission of or in connection with an offence under the MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, it is not always conclusive at first instance if a vehicle is linked to the offence and further investigations after seizure are often needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, these are operational matters, and we want to make it consistent and practical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These amendments align the position in the MDA with the powers of investigation provided for under the CPC that are conferred on CNB officers when investigating drug offences, which enables seizure based on suspicion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Another set of amendments pertains to the provisions concerning drug abusers charged under the Singapore Armed Forces Act 1972, or the SAF Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These amendments aim to clarify the policy intent for provisions in the MDA concerning enhanced punishments and supervision for drug abusers convicted under the SAF Act and improve consistency between both regimes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Currently, SAF servicemen caught for drug consumption may be charged under section 26 of the SAF Act or section 34 of the SAF Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Section 34 of the SAF Act may also be used to charge SAF servicemen for drug possession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Similarly, clause 26 clarifies that only antecedents for drug consumption under section 34 of the SAF Act, will count towards long-term imprisonment under section 33A of the MDA for the repeat consumption of specified drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Separately, section 58(1)(q) currently allows the Minister for Home Affairs to make regulations in respect of the supervision and aftercare of persons convicted of an offence under section 34 of the SAF Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, there is no similar provision for the Minister to make regulations in respect of persons convicted of an offence under section 26 of the SAF Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 30 amends section 58(1)(q) to include those convicted under section 26 of the SAF Act for drug consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Since there is a separate rehabilitation regime implemented by the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) for drug abusers convicted under section 26 of the SAF Act, such offenders would generally not be placed under CNB's supervision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Section 58(1)(q) is further amended to make clear that the Minister's powers to make regulations providing for the supervision and aftercare of persons convicted under section 34 of the SAF Act, relate only to those convicted under the section for drug consumption and not for drug possession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will also make amendments to broaden the scope of the recall provision under section 31(1A) of the MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Currently, section 31(1A) allows the Director of CNB to recall any former drug abuser to report for a urine test, throughout the person’s life, to ensure that the person is no longer a drug addict.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 21 amends the definition of "relevant person" and "relevant time" in section 31, to include persons convicted under section 26 of the SAF Act for the consumption of a controlled drug or psychoactive substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will also amend section 31 so that a person who has been convicted under section 34 of the SAF Act for an offence involving consumption of a controlled drug or psychoactive substance can be subjected to the recall provision, even if he had not previously undergone CNB's supervision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In short, with these amendments, the Director of CNB will be able to recall and subject any person who has been convicted for drug consumption under the SAF Act to a urine test.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, the proposed amendments to the MDA will help us to stay ahead of the changing drug landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: First, we will be changing the approach toward controlling psychoactive substances, so that we can act quicker against them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Second, we will increase the punishment for the possession of large quantities of selected controlled drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: NPS are a challenge to law enforcement agencies around the world, as drug syndicates are able to quickly alter the molecular structure of NPS to create new variants and, hence, evade the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Currently, we manage NPS in the following ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Once we detect an NPS, we will list its molecular structure in the Fifth Schedule of the MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The MDA allows for such listing up to a year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: During this one-year period, CNB can seize the substance to prevent its proliferation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: CNB will use this time to conduct industry consultations to determine if the substance has any legitimate uses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: During this one-year period, CNB cannot take any prosecutorial action against a person trafficking in the substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If there are no legitimate uses, the molecular structure of this substance will subsequently be listed in the First Schedule to the MDA as a controlled drug.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Only when it is listed in the First Schedule, can a person who is found trafficking, manufacturing, importing, exporting or possessing such NPS, be prosecuted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The failing of the current approach is that we will always be playing catch-up with the syndicates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The ease in modifying the molecular structure of NPS to create new variants means that traffickers can easily overcome our laws by switching to new, unlisted NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This allows CNB to take enforcement action against potentially dangerous and potent NPS, and not have to wait until their molecular structure has been identified and listed in the MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The second key amendment is to increase and tier punishments for possessing large quantities of selected controlled drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These are drugs which we assess to be the most dangerous and harmful in Singapore's context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: With these changes to our laws, we can be more effective in our fight against drugs and in keeping our society free from drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: (In English): In addition to the amendment related to treatment and rehabilitation for abusers of psychoactive substances, there are two other amendments to the Constitution made through the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Technical amendments are made to clauses (4) and (6)(b) of Article 46, replacing the word "leave" with "permission".

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is consistent with the same amendment made in other Acts by the Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Act 2021.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There is no change to the meaning of the provisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had, during the Budget Statement in February, said that the Government will introduce a mechanism to reduce the balance of the Contingencies Funds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The objective is to maintain discipline in how the Government manages its finances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In May 2020, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, MOF raised the Contingencies Funds balance from $3 billion to $16 billion to enable the Government to meet urgent and unforeseen spending needs arising from the fast-evolving pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This was done by appropriating monies from the Consolidated Fund through the Second Supplementary Supply (FY2020) Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, there is no legal mechanism today to effect a reduction of the balances to ensure fiscal discipline as we return to normalcy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Minister is also required to present to Parliament a report of every reduction as soon as practicable after it is made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This will keep Members informed of the balance of the Contingencies Funds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The transfer of sums from a Contingencies Fund to the Consolidated or Development Fund does not provide the Government with additional budget for spending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Government will need to run a balanced Budget over its term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Any expenditure from the Consolidated Fund or Development Fund must be met by revenues raised and included in a Supply Bill that is presented to Parliament for approval.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Such spending remains subject to the Reserves Protection Framework.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: NPS have become a global phenomenon with 139 countries affected, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As at December 2022, more than 1,182 substances have been reported.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: NPS are just as addictive and mimic the effects of controlled substances, such as cannabis, cocaine and heroin.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: NPS is proliferating at an unprecedented rate and poses a challenge for law enforcement worldwide.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: NPS are one of the three most abused types of drugs since 2018; and NPS overtook cannabis in 2019 as the second-most commonly abused type of drugs among new abusers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Listing NPS as controlled drugs is a challenge in all jurisdictions because we need to keep up with the fast pace of development of NPS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In order for the substances to be listed in the First Schedule of the MDA, the relevant scientific analysis on the chemical structure and necessary industry consultations have to be done to determine whether or not there is a legitimate use for such substances and if there is no such legitimate use, the NPS will be listed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This means that during the interim period when the NPS is unlisted, enforcement and prosecutorial actions cannot be taken against those who deal in those substances.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, the lag time allows NPS manufacturers time to develop alternative substances or deliberately alter the chemical structures to circumvent our drug control legislation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do have two clarifications: one, on the defence for legitimate use; second, the other on the presumptions of possession and knowledge of NPS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill provides a defence if the psychoactive substance is intended to be used for a legitimate purpose other than for human consumption.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under the new sections 11F to 11P, the person must have the intention or reasons to believe such a legitimate purpose, in various scenarios, including where an accused believed that the other party had intended to manufacture the psychoactive substance for a legitimate purpose.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, a person who breaches such regulations or falls short of certain standards should not be allowed to avail himself of this defence of legitimate purpose.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A person who has control or custody of anything containing psychoactive substances or keys to a place where such psychoactive substances are found under the new section 18A, will be presumed to have had those psychoactive substances in his or her possession.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This then triggers separate presumptions of knowledge in the new section 18A(2), read with the new section 22B, namely two separate presumptions: firstly, that person is presumed to have known that the substance has the capacity to have a psychoactive effect on an individual if consumed; and secondly, the person is presumed as not believing nor having any reason to believe that the psychoactive substance is an excluded substance.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What due diligence is one expected to do and conduct in such circumstances?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   NPS have become widespread all over the world and they mimic the effects of drugs, such as marijuana, opium and heroin.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Due to its variable chemical structure, detecting NPS becomes increasingly difficult.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, the number of NPS drug users has increased.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This legislative framework updates the list of NPS and how new NPS can be detected in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Apart from NPS, drugs, such as marijuana and methamphetamine, are dangerous and threaten the peace and security of our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fifteen grammes of diamorphine alone, is enough to satisfy the addiction of 180 people for a week.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Imagine how many families and children will be affected by one case alone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must always be vigilant and determined in eradicating drugs in our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This toughens our stance against drug abuse and makes clear the already tough sentencing guidelines laid down by our courts since the case of Lai Teck Guan by Chief Justice Menon.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The sentencing must be commensurate to the harm that large quantities of drugs pose.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some may argue that weight of a drug alone is not an accurate factor to determine the level of harm posed, and one should refer to the potency of addiction instead.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, until and unless there is a reliable technology to determine such potency accurately and independently, weight remains a useful barometer.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This tough stance against drugs is needed to protect the vulnerable groups in our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recently, last month, it was reported that CNB arrested a 32-year-old woman for drug offences.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In June last year, a nine-month-old baby was found with his drug abuser mother in dire living conditions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: CNB officers provided childcare necessities and milk powder for the baby.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These are sad and tragic cases and I am glad that Singapore adopts a strong stance to protect our vulnerable groups and, hopefully, prevent such cases in future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: According to CNB, 26% of all drug abusers arrested were below 30 years old.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Out of all the new abusers arrested, half of them were aged below 30.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, we need to be wary of the prevalence of the vaping culture trend worldwide.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While nicotine is commonly consumed through vaping, these cigarettes can also be used as a way to deliver other controlled drugs, such as methamphetamine and heroin.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, vaping has become a common way of inhaling cannabis.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Canada, 29% of cannabis-using individuals aged 15 years and older, indicated that vaping is their preferred method for cannabis use.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is a strong link and risk between vaping use and drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although it is already illegal here, we need to step up on enforcement and education on the harms of vaping.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Vaping instruments also come in various shapes and forms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He was introduced to drugs by people who knew of his precarious emotional state and took advantage of him to lure him into addiction.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Once hooked, he had to pay through his nose, sometimes four or five times higher than the drug's street value, in order to avoid being detected or recognised.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He has since served his time and rehabilitated himself.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He now volunteers in the Anti-Drug Abuse Advocacy A3 Network with the National Council Against Drug Abuse (NCADA) and CNB.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a young and successful professional, he may not fit the mould of a stereotypical drug abuser.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: His story shows that our fight against drug abuse must be made on behalf of every segment of our society – our youths, our children, our workers – and we face battlefronts everywhere – our schools, our workplaces, our homes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Drug traffickers drive addiction to feed their greed for profits, at the expense of families and communities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They will continue to introduce new drugs and new ways to circumvent our laws and influence our people, but just as they are relentless in their ways, we must, similarly, be tireless in our vigilance to protect the minds and safety of our people, steward the future and potential of our youths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this fight against drugs, we cannot let them win.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There has been rapid development of new synthetic substances with narcotic or psychotropic effects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These effects are reportedly similar to those of drugs, such as cocaine and cannabis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Most of these substances also carry a risk of addiction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As these new substances may fall outside the ambit of existing drug laws, those taking them are able to get "legal highs", which accounts for their demand.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a vast array of new substances, with some more harmful than others.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To assist governments to decide which substances to regulate, UNODC has been sharing toxicology information with laboratories and governments, highlighting the substances deemed more harmful to the individual and social health.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have seen families whose lives have been upended by drug addiction, with cross-generational effects, such as absent parents and young children growing up in institutional care.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We owe it to Singaporeans to minimise such scenarios.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This includes providing a regime for the supervision, treatment and rehabilitation of NPS abusers, without charging them in court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I would like to seek two clarifications on the new framework to regulate NPS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Out of the thousands of psychoactive substances, how will the Ministry decide which ones to regulate?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides the UNODC advice, are there other forms of reference?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My second query, relates to the listing of NPS as controlled drugs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: NPS are currently listed in the First Schedule to the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister of State earlier stated the Ministry's concern that, due to the rapid emergence of new substances, there will be a time lag of about one year before these substances are listed as prohibited.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During this interim, law enforcement and prosecution agencies are currently powerless to act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Hence, the Ministry is introducing this Bill to enable agencies to act on a more general definition of what counts as a psychoactive substance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry confirm that it is the intention to list every NPS of interest in the First Schedule to the MDA?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Put another way, how will we handle cases where someone is investigated for an NPS offence, based on the general broad definition, but the substance concerned is eventually found after industry consultation to have a legitimate use?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is good for the Minister of State to explain this, because, I think, earlier in his Second Reading speech, he mentioned that if such a legitimate use were to be determined, then such a substance would not be listed in the Schedule to the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, some clarity on this would be quite necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to why this change is being tabled, the Ministry has stated that CNB have observed that abusers were purchasing larger quantities of drugs, which would have "significantly contributed to the local drug demand situation".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The changes will separate the punishments into three tiers, depending on the weight of the drugs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the lowest tier of weight, no change to the punishment is being made.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the middle and upper tiers, the punishments are being enhanced.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In trying to make sense of this, I studied the changes relating to the possession of diamorphine, or heroin.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note that, under the existing law, there is a presumption that a person is a drug trafficker once he is in possession of more than two grammes of diamorphine.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this Bill, the lowest tier of punishment for diamorphine cuts off at a maximum of 10 grammes – much higher than two grammes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: No change in punishment for this tier is being proposed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For these two higher tiers, the punishments for possession are being increased.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is important for the Ministry to justify these increases and elaborate on the local drug demand situation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further, would it be correct to infer that these changes are actually targeted at cases where the suspects are charged with trafficking, but the trafficking charges somewhat fail in court?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our strict anti-drug policies have broad-based support among Singaporeans, especially those who have lived through the earlier years when heroin and opium destroyed many families.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, there appears to be a desire in some segments of the population for a more nuanced approach, especially towards younger people who are influenced by peers to try drugs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is not an approach I would advocate, but it will be important to engage with such sentiments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Member Mr Zhulkarnain made a similar point earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now move to the Constitution (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 2 concerns the amendments to the MDA, while clause 4 seeks to plug what the Finance Ministry sees as a gap in the law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As regards clause 2, as mentioned earlier, the Workers' Party supports the rationale for tackling NPS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The MDA Bill envisaged a supervision, treatment and rehabilitation regime that may involve the detention of individuals without a court conviction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, in this specific circumstance, we are able to support the amendment to Article 9 to give effect to the treatment regime for NPS misuse.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now move on to clause 4 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is an amendment to Article 148C, concerning the powers of the Finance Minister to make transfers between the Consolidated Fund and its Contingencies Fund, and between the Development Fund and its Contingencies Fund.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He assessed that this would ensure adequate resources for exigencies, while retaining discipline in how our finances were managed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He then highlighted that this Constitutional amendment was needed, as there was currently no mechanism for a reduction of the balances of the Contingencies Funds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are two new sub-articles being introduced to Article 148(c).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will be allowed if the Minister, after proper inquiry, is satisfied that the sum to be transferred back is an excess of what is likely necessary to meet an urgent and unforeseen need from that Contingencies Fund.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Logically, there is no reason for us to object to a transfer back of the sums to the Consolidated Fund and Development Fund, if these are assessed to be no longer needed for contingencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, it is useful for the Minister to clarify the role of Parliament in this process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the May 2020 debate on the Fortitude Budget, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat had explained the role of Parliament when it came to drawing on the balance in the Contingencies Funds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He highlighted that any amount advanced by the Minister for Finance to meet urgent expenditure would thereafter be included in a Supplementary Supply Bill or Final Supply Bill, which would be presented to and voted on by Parliament as soon as practicable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is an important process as Parliament is briefed on the items being spent on and will vote on whether to pass the Bills or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In today's Constitution (Amendment) Bill, we are dealing with a situation where excess monies parked in the Contingencies Funds are being returned to their parent funds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Manufacturers of NPS circumvent the existing legal framework by altering the chemical structure of the substances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The burden is, then, on the individual to prove that the psychoactive substance is an excluded substance on a balance of probabilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Excluded substances include alcohol, food, health products and herbal medicines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify, what exactly it is that the individual is required to prove?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is the individual required to prove that the substance is factually an excluded substance, or is it sufficient for the individual to prove that they had reason to believe that the substance is an excluded substance?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the new provisions of "stacked" presumptions. "Stacked" presumptions occur where proof of a single element triggers multiple presumptions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If an individual has the keys to a place where a psychoactive substance is found, the individual is presumed to have possession of the psychoactive substance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the individual is presumed to have possession, the individual is also presumed to have known that the psychoactive substance has the capacity to produce a psychoactive effect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The individual is also presumed to not believe that the psychoactive substance is an excluded substance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, the presumptions are not rebutted by proof that the accused never had physical possession of the psychoactive substance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such stacked presumptions are not new under the MDA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, they are still concerning because they challenge the traditional position that the prosecution must prove every element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Stacked presumptions may be even more concerning when applied to NPS, which covers non-exhaustive categories of substances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify, what would be required to rebut stacked presumptions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point, is on the enforcement of our drug laws through drug raids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that we have strong drug laws and that these laws are enforced robustly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, innocent children may be implicated when their parents are caught up in drug raids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These drug raids can be traumatising for the children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The next generation should not be punished or traumatised because of the wrongs of the previous generation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Despite the challenges with taking such a strong stance on drugs, I have always held to my strong conviction that this is the best way to protect Singapore and protect families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have spoken before, of our continuing need to review our MDA to tackle new and emerging threats, particularly NPS because of how fast such substances evolve and arrive on our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I am greatly heartened to see the Ministry grabbing the bull by its horns and pre-emptively creating this new regime and statutory framework to regulate psychoactive substances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The threat that NPS pose cannot be underestimated – and I speak not just about the situation in Singapore, but globally, because drugs are a transnational issue that we must collectively combat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is because a simple modification to the chemical structure can result in a new variant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The report detailed the global increase in countries reporting seizures of synthetic NPS, indicating a far greater geographical spread of trafficking.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2009 to 2010, only 30 countries were reporting seizures of synthetic NPS.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By 2019 to 2020, that number had increased to 57 countries – a jump from 18% of countries reporting, to 41% of countries reporting.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not only do NPS evolve rapidly, Asia accounts for a large percentage of the NPS being trafficked.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, the largest quantities of synthetic NPS seized is ketamine, with a lot of the seizures happening in East and Southeast Asia, in countries like Malaysia, Thailand and China.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the market for ketamine for non-medical use seems to have decreased in China, there has been a trend of expansion of the ketamine market since 2015 in the rest of Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Plant-based NPS, like kratom and khat, have also been proliferating with more countries reporting seizure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The largest seizures for kratom, has been in Malaysia, Thailand and Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are but some of the most seized NPS, but there are many more also used and likely on the rise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indonesia has seen a sharp increase in seizures of domestically manufactured synthetic cannabinoids and what is known as "gorilla tobacco".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This prevalence is highly concerning, especially so, because the global trend is that NPS use is about 2.2% higher among school populations than the general population.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, NPS cause just as much harm as other drugs, with physical and psychological reactions, such as paranoia, seizures, hallucinations and even death.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It continues the Ministry of Home Affairs' and CNB's long-standing efforts to combat the rise of NPS.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2010, we first listed three NPS under MDA.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2013, we introduced a more generic listing approach, given the chemical similarity between different NPS.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we have continued to look at our statutory provisions and considered how we may best strengthen them to protect against any tolerance of NPS.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The amendment Bill, then, is a welcome addition and I applaud MHA and CNB for their work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With Part 2 specifically listing out offences relating to NPS, we are able to target the trafficking, manufacturing and importing of NPS.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, this includes offences of exposing a child to NPS or permitting a young person to consume NPS.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also support the change in the Fifth Schedule.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By listing what substances are excluded from the definition of an NPS, it creates a much broader ambit since now any substance not listed within the Fifth Schedule can be captured.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This squarely deals with the proliferation of NPS variants such that MDA need not be constantly updated, which would be too lengthy a process and ill-equipped to handle the fast-paced nature of the NPS market.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In relation to that, clause 32 of the amendment Bill seeking to enhance the Minister's ability to amend the Schedule under section 59, will reflect this pre-emptive regime we are putting in place to tackle NPS.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must recognise that NPS is a growing market and today's amendment Bill reflects that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we should also place keen emphasis on rehabilitation so that we build a stronger social compact of individuals who have no desire for any sort of substance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, the role of rehabilitation in integrating those who have fallen afoul of our drug laws back into society, by giving them second chances, is crucial.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is done through programmes for the public or education institutions to interact with former offenders and increasing their employability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the end of the day, a former drug abuser has to not only leave a physical prison but break out of a social prison in order to reintegrate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lowering these invisible bars of prejudice and suspicion and providing them opportunities to be mentored will allow young drug abusers to transform and overcome their rough start.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It provides for future flexibility to continue to evolve quickly to changes in the illicit NPS market.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For all these reasons, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, such deterrence alone is not sufficient, as we can still see these activities going on with impudence despite the harsh penalties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will also need to consider how we can successfully flush out such syndicates operating in the region and their distribution channels into Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The UN had repeatedly appealed to governments, especially those in Asia, to consider the problem of the abuse of and trafficking in amphetamine-type stimulants in their entirety, including their prevalence and the reasons why more youths in the region are turning to the abuse of methamphetamine.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This problem is a regional issue and every country has a part to play in slowing down this drug epidemic.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there regional information sharing partnerships that can be enhanced?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will invariably undermine existing efforts as the attitudes of youths in the region towards drugs will also shift.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the advent of NPS, we are not simply saddled with a drug issue, but it also translates into community mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   With the advent of NPS, we are not simply saddled with a drug issue, but it also translates into community mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Studies have shown that substance abuse and mental health issues are often co-occurring disorders, and abusers require long-term support, treatment and guidance in order to have a better chance at rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, can I request for more comprehensive and longer-term mental health resources and support for drug abusers who have gone through rehabilitation?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This contrasts with the increasingly softer approach taken by more and more countries globally and in the region, including our neighbours in ASEAN, where Thailand has decriminalised and legalised cannabis.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Media reports have highlighted that Malaysia is also aiming to learn from Thailand's cannabis policy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I read the  UNODC report in June 2022.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What drew my attention was that the legalisation of cannabis in North America had led to increased tax revenues and fewer arrests.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What was even alarming for me was that cannabis use, particularly by the young, increased and co-related with psychiatric disorders, suicides and hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It appears that they have traded short-term gains for negative longer-term impact on their society.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is a path we cannot afford to take.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, I am heartened by MHA's commitment to ensure our drug policies are robust and relevant to deal with evolving trends, such as the advent of  NPS, especially given the reopening of borders and the rebound of overseas travel.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I raised this as Singapore adopts an evidence-based approach and has allowed the use of cannabis-derived medication in exceptional cases of drug-resistant epilepsy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the Bill provides for an accused to be able to invoke a defence by proving that he/she intended or believed that the psychoactive substance would be used for a legitimate purpose, other than for human consumption.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding that the burden of proof is on the defendant, can the Minister clarify if and/or how agencies' resources will be expended in the validation of such claims by accused persons in such a defence, as well as the safeguards against attempts to frustrate justice?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As with all policies, it is imperative for legislation to be coupled with effective implementation to achieve intended outcomes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, beyond the Bill, what is equally important is to continue strengthening our agencies' detective and intervention capabilities against substance abuse.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, I was glad to hear about the new saliva test kit for drugs, as shared by Minister of State Faishal at MHA's Committee of Supply (COS) debate and its deployment at checkpoints and roadblocks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If not, are there plans to explore having similar efficient testing methods for NPS, to enhance on-ground detection as well as deterrence?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, a public that is aware of the harms of drugs and NPS remains our first line of defence.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I seek the Minister's clarification on the plan to better equip and educate the public on NPS, like how to spot them, so that they too can notify enforcement agencies and amplify efforts to combat the scourge of new forms of drugs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the Minister, earlier, shared statistics on the increased use of NPS.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These statistics and trends, I believe, may also assist the public engagement effort by driving home the message that NPS are posing a real and credible threat within our society.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: They are necessary to keep Singapore crime rates low and help minimise the impact to the lives of Singaporeans that have been marred by drug abuse.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Liberal and conservative views towards drugs describe little about the underlying human condition that fuels the necessity of today's debate here in this Chamber, namely, addiction.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Regardless of society's personal attitudes and perspectives on drugs, addiction is a problem that needs societal attention going beyond punitive measures.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we seek to tackle the supply-side issues through this Bill, my suggestions are rooted in supplementing the punitive measures with programmes and rehabilitation that tackle the issue of demand fueled by addiction.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The effect of this amendment is that a person who is addicted to a psychoactive substance may be committed to supervision, treatment or rehabilitation under section 34.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is aligned with existing powers with respect to controlled drugs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I remember a photograph and some headlines in June 2022, which said that a baby was found in a squalid flat close to his mother during a recent drug bust.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was reported that his mother was a user.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While majority agreed that drugs are harmful and supported a drug-free Singapore, some went further to call the mother heartless, useless and condemned her, among other terms that I cannot reproduce here.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most people saw, first, a mother who was irresponsible, as she was a user.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A few looked at the photograph with a slightly different lens and saw a user who was struggling with her addiction, yet doing the best that she could to still be a mother.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do not know either mother or child.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But hope that both are getting the support and care that they need.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If you cannot bond with society healthily because you are traumatised or beaten down by life, you may be born with something else that gives you a sense of relief.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People who develop addictions are often looked at society, as being a person that has developed a fatal character flaw.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, research has shown that addiction is a medical condition that is often linked to undesirable conditions that create the disposition in the very first place and has the propensity to develop in the absence of a healthy environment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A classic study conducted on soldiers integrating back into society post-war in Vietnam by Lee and Robins, followed soldiers who used heroin heavily during the war after they returned home.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order to track if that translated into lifelong addictions, the data in the study found that environmental and social factors had a core relative effect on the soldier's decision to continue to abuse drugs after coming back from the war.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Soldiers who came back to families and support structures were less likely to abuse drugs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, drug addiction remains a complex issue, having an adverse impact on individuals, families and society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the years, the Government has implemented a range of rehabilitation programmes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope we can continue to enhance our rehabilitative approaches, in particular, programmes need to take into account evolving research and the complex and evolving environmental circumstances of drug addicts in order to provide personalised support.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our current rehabilitation programmes, such as programmes by the DRC, Community Rehabilitation Centre and the National Addictions Management Service, there is already significant detachment from a one-size-fit-all approach.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I welcome this, taking into account the fact that each individual's experience with drugs and addiction is unique and as such, treatment should be tailored to their specific needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, some may require more intensive counselling, some may benefit more from group therapy or medical interventions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is salient, as research has shown that the lack of personalised support results in a lower success rate for rehabilitation programmes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, how does the Government seek to improve the efficiency of these support initiatives by pairing it with harm reduction strategies, like overdose prevention programmes and medication assisted treatment?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Further, the lack of sustained longer-term support may lead to an addict's relapse and disappointment by loved ones, ultimately straining relationships and exacerbating addiction.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The guiding aim of what I have mentioned will be to provide individuals with the tools to reduce the harm associated with drug use, keeping them safe and consistent as they work towards recovery, as we know that change does not occur overnight.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: According to statistics by CNB, drug abuse among our youth has declined since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The correlation between mental health challenges and drug use cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People self-medicate in an attempt to feel better and often end up exacerbating the symptoms of the very condition that they are trying to sooth.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Collaboration between schools, communities and youth networks may help the development of a "Spot, Identify and Intervene" framework that could prevent the development of addiction to substances.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must also recognise the aetiology of mental health issues, such as inadequate supervision, lack of consistency in home environments, frequent parent conflicts, domestic violence, and so forth.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A child growing up in these circumstances will not solely be deterred by the proverbial stick.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I applaud further measures to safeguard our young population from the dangers of drugs and NPS addictions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In an effort to evade legal restrictions, drug manufacturers have resorted to synthesising substances that mimic the effects of conventional drugs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moreover, the adolescent demographic may be particularly vulnerable to succumbing to peer pressure or experimenting with illicit substances due to a lack of awareness or understanding of trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, provisions in part 2(A), such as section 11(n), 11(p) and 11(q), are appropriate.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Attempts to shield our youth from being exposed to drug-related information while important, also needs to be realistic.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Information permeates through phones and contradicting narratives and perspectives of drugs can easily be found online.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is helpful to communicate in commonly accepted direct narratives, rather than blanket statements.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, substance addiction often leaves the addict in a place where they lose agency over their lives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Efforts such as "Finding Juliana", a TikTok campaign by NCADA illustrate this point well.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, we need to be proactive in our approach to help those who have not yet fallen prey to drug addiction but are still at risk.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Previously, I have volunteered with younger girls in Reformative Training Centres (RTCs) and often left prisons worrying about the conditions that they would meet post-release.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Financial challenges and poor familial relations as well as sometimes parents who were users themselves, I hope we can further study the issue of vulnerable youths and inter-generational addiction so that effective and timely support can be extended to them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To conclude, it is imperative that policies aimed at addressing misuse of substances continue to account for the multifaceted circumstances that contribute to this.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is only by taking a whole-of-society approach and effectively addressing both supply and demand for illicit substances, that we can protect our people from the pain and suffering cause by substance addictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Ms Lim rightly noted, logically, there is no reason to object.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She felt that it would be useful for the Minister to clarify the role of Parliament in the process and what form it would take, and how Members can participate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They merely reflect how we classify the Government's resources for specified objectives, in accordance with the laws governing each fund, for the purposes of accounting and reporting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the form that it would take.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Perhaps, Ms Sylvia Lim, we can take clarifications later.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As Mr Ng pointed out, the use of presumptions and the application of more than one presumption acting on the same set of facts, is not new under the MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We should remember that the fundamental reason for the use of presumptions in drug offences is because the facts, which are being presumed, are often exclusively within the accused persons' knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In the example given by Mr Ng relating to having a key to a place, the presumption places the onus on the person found in possession of such a key to explain why he did not know the drugs were there, in spite of having the key to that particular place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Where there is no presumption, the burden is generally placed on the prosecution to prove a fact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Our long experience in dealing with drug trafficking syndicates is that without legal tools, such as presumptions, drug traffickers will be able to evade legal responsibility by simply saying that they did not know the drugs were there or they did not know what they were carrying.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
