text: The drug mules in the past, and still today, are trained to say certain things upon arrest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The prosecution, despite having proven that the drugs were in the accused persons' possession, are often not able to prove the accused person's knowledge of the drugs beyond a reasonable doubt, so long as he simply says that he did not know the nature of the drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Without them, we would not have been able to keep the drug trafficking situation in Singapore under control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We would also have, otherwise, only been able to punish people who came clean and confessed to the offences, while the guilty traffickers who lied to the authorities would go free.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I would add that there are other presumptions, which have also worked well for other offences, such as the presumption that a person whose urine test is positive, is presumed to have consumed drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Legally, the presumptions can be rebutted; and, historically, they have been rebutted many times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Whether the presumption can be rebutted turns on whether the accused's account is to be believed or not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He cannot simply say he did not know, or he did not care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The facts or evidence required to rebut the presumption, would very much depend on the nature of the defence raised by the individual and a credibility of his account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The issue of more than one presumption acting on the same set of facts has been raised in the past, because the presumptions in the MDA presume different facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: More than one presumption can be triggered in respect of one set of facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, if an individual possesses the keys to anything containing a controlled drug, he can be presumed to have that drug in his possession and also presumed to know the nature of that drug.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, the presumption cannot be used unfairly to prejudice the accused.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, the presumptions of possession and knowledge cannot be invoked together with the presumption of trafficking, as these presumptions each serve a different function.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Courts are careful to ensure that the burden on the accused is not so onerous, that it becomes virtually impossible to discharge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Court of Appeal has said that, notwithstanding the use of presumptions, innocent persons can prove their innocence without any difficulty; whilst guilty persons cannot avoid liability by merely asserting a lack of knowledge without more, therefore undermining the general policy of the MDA itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In fact, the Courts have also said that the MDA presumptions strike an appropriate balance between the rights of the accused persons on the one hand; and the rights of the persons in the wider society on the other, who would otherwise be adversely and directly infected by the availability of drugs on the open market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While I understand Mr Ng's concern, it is incorrect to state that the application of the MDA presumptions is more concerning when applied to NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The presumptions operate in the same way, to presume facts that are especially within the accused's knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To address Mr Ng's related question on this, an individual who claims that the substance is an excluded substance can either prove factually that the substance is an excluded substance; or where the section 18A(2) presumption applies, prove that he believed and had reason to believe that the substance was an excluded substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These defences are not applicable to traditional controlled drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We believe our proposed approach straddles an appropriate balance between ensuring that those who are in possession of NPS for illegal purposes can be dealt with under the law, while, at the same time, ensuring that those who are innocent can show this without an unfair burden on them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On the same topic of presumptions, Mr Zulkarnain asked about the safeguards in place to protect innocent landlords.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: During the investigation, CNB will establish who was in the possession of the drugs and how the drugs came to be at a particular location.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: CNB or AGC do not simply prefer charges against people who own properties and rely on the presumptions to prove their case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In any event, as we have controlled drugs under the current law, an innocent landlord can easily rebut the presumption of possession by proving on a balance of probabilities that the psychoactive substance was not in his possession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To do so, the innocent landlord could, for instance, point to the fact that a third-party occupier had full access and control over the property in question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Alternatively, if the innocent landlord was in possession of the item, but did not know of its nature, he could then rebut the presumption of knowledge by, for example, explaining that he did not know that the item has a psychoactive effect when consumed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Namely, knowledge that a substance is, in fact, a psychoactive substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, I hope I have addressed all the issues about presumptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Next, I would like to thank Mr Derrick Goh, Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Zhulkarnain for their questions on the new control regime for NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, with this new framework, all newly discovered psychoactive substances will be subject to the new legislative framework by default.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: CNB can take action against persons dealing with them unless the substance is excluded under the Fifth Schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Specifically, to address Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Derrick Goh's question on the processes undertaken by MHA before listing newly discovered substances under the First Schedule or Fifth Schedule of MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If a newly discovered psychoactive substance intended for abuse emerges in the local market or is identified for international control by UNODC, CNB will, indeed, seek to list it in the First Schedule of MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Before listing, CNB will work with HTX and HSA to conduct rigorous testing and industry consultations to ascertain if the substance has legitimate purposes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If the substance is found not to have any legitimate uses, it will be listed as a controlled drug in the First Schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is the same approach adopted currently for substances we list under the First Schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This took approximately eight months for the necessary testing, verification and legislative amendments to be carried out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For completeness, to answer Ms Sylvia Lim's question if MHA intends to eventually list all psychoactive substances that are found to have no legitimate uses and intended for abuse under the First Schedule, the answer is: yes, we do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We hope for MDA to be as comprehensive in its coverage of these harmful substances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If the new substance is found to have legitimate uses or is regulated under other existing laws or regulations, it will be listed under the Fifth Schedule, as an excluded substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The frequency of such listings will depend on the emergence of new substances in the market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If a newly discovered substance is legitimately being used for scientific or medical research purposes and this can be proven with supporting evidence, such research activities would not constitute offences under the new regime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If, as in Mr Zhulkarnain's example, a person is found to have failed to comply with the expected standards in the handling of a psychoactive substance for legitimate purposes, like for medical research, they will not be prosecuted under MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They may, instead, be taken to task by the relevant governing authority or Ministry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To reiterate, the amendments are not meant to target legitimate substances or activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Instead, it is aimed at psychoactive substances created for the purposes of abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On Mr Derrick Goh's question of resources expended in verifying an accused person's defence that the NPS he is dealing with has legitimate uses, I wish to emphasise that the current provision specifies that the accused bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the substance, indeed, had legitimate uses other than for human consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It would not be for CNB or the prosecution to prove or disprove his claim.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This would prevent persons from attempting to employ such a defence without sufficient basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Derrick Goh also asked if the new saliva test kits can detect NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While there are commercially available test kits that can detect certain classes of NPS, this would not be exhaustive due to the sheer number and diversity of NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The test kits used by CNB, are meant as a screening tool and are able to detect the key controlled drugs that are commonly abused in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Nevertheless, CNB will continue to monitor NPS trends and, with advancements in technology, CNB will be able to assess the feasibility of deploying more comprehensive test kits that are capable of detecting more NPS in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I cannot agree more with Mr Derrick Goh's point on the importance of preventive drug education (PDE) and keeping the public informed of NPS trends.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Since the emergence of NPS abuse in Singapore, CNB has been proactively publishing informational brochures on NPS and their harms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: CNB also engages the youth within schools and through those in positions of influence over youths, such as parents, counsellors, educators, youth advocates and National Service commanders, to educate them on NPS and their harms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I would also caution that if anyone is unsure if he is in possession of a psychoactive substance, he should undertake reasonable means to find out what is the nature of and the intended purpose of the substance in question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, by asking the person who gave him the substance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If the person continues to be unsure, he should report this to CNB or the Police immediately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked about statistics of youths abusing NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In my opening speech, I provided NPS abuse numbers in the last five years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Goh may wish to refer to the annual statistics release published by CNB that provides a more detailed profile of drug abusers arrested by drug type, including NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We cannot afford to be caught on the backfoot and only take action when NPS abuse becomes pervasive in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether the amendments to introduce a tiered punishment framework for the drug possession offence are targeted at cases where the persons are charged with trafficking but the trafficking charge fails in Court.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The question of whether charges would be preferred for trafficking or for possession would be determined by the facts, as established by the investigations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked for further justifications on why we need to increase the penalties for possession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Hence, that is why we want to be proactive to deter local possession of large quantities of drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Joan Pereira rightly pointed out Singapore's vulnerability to the threat of drug trafficking, due to its transnational nature, and asked if regional information sharing partnerships can be enhanced and the role Singapore plays in committing some resources to such efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: CNB actively participates in international and regional efforts for information sharing and operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, CNB is part of the ASEAN Airport and Seaport Interdiction Task Forces, which provide platforms for enforcement agencies to collaborate and interdict drug trafficking in the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: CNB also works closely with its overseas counterparts to share intelligence, and this has resulted in significant arrests and seizures both locally and overseas over the past years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In 2022, CNB also organised an inaugural workshop on Singapore's Drug Control Strategy for our international counterparts to contribute to their capacity-building and promote cooperation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Such cooperation has been crucial in helping to keep the threat of drugs at bay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Specifically for NPS, information sharing in the region has allowed countries to quickly list NPS for control once they have first been detected in one country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, this has been very helpful because we want to make sure that we protect everyone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Many countries would like to play a part in this and see how we can reduce the harms to the people and prevent such happenings occurring in our jurisdiction as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This will allow us to have a bigger voice in shaping international drug-control policies and sharing our best practices on a global stage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether MHA works with MSF and social service agencies to ensure that children of drug-offending parents are cared for appropriately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will not go into a detailed reply as this topic has been discussed in the House before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There is currently a referral process between CNB and MSF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: CNB officers can conduct early identification of family members at the scene of arrest and make the necessary referrals to MSF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is something that we have been enhancing, deepening; and our relationship with our agencies has become much better, so that we are able to help more and more Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked what MHA is doing in concert with HSA and other Ministries to address vaping.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This topic was discussed at MOH's Committee of Supply debate earlier this month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: MHA works with MOH, the Ministry of Education (MOE), HSA and other agencies through the National Committee on Prevention, Rehabilitation and Recidivism, NCPR in short, to tackle the problem of substance abuse, particularly amongst youths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This issue is something that we work together on and it is something that, if you look back at the history, we have been doing for many decades and we will continue to enhance this effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We share his passion and commitment, and we are very happy to have someone like him journeying with us to keep Singapore drug-free.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While we strengthen our enforcement framework against drugs with these amendments, MHA is still committed to ensuring that drug abusers receive the rehabilitation they require.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked if the Government can provide more personalised support to recovering drug addicts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Similarly, Ms Joan Pereira asked if more comprehensive and long-term mental health resources and support could be offered to drug abusers who have gone through rehabilitation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Some ex-drug abusers struggle with mental illness or juggle multiple stressors, such as securing employment or managing strained family relationships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: During the time that an ex-drug abuser is placed on CNB's supervision, the CNB supervision officer assigned to the ex-drug abuser will regularly check in on his or her well-being and assess their reintegration needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The supervision officer will make referrals to social service agencies, such as Family Service Centres, to provide further support for their mental, psycho-social and other needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As Ms Nadia Samdin has pointed out, our current rehabilitation programmes take a calibrated approach based on the individual's risks and needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: At the same time, CNB and Prisons conduct regular reviews, including with MSF, to determine what more can be done to support ex-drug abusers in their rehabilitation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia also asked if MHA would consider adopting harm reduction strategies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: At the 2018 Committee of Supply debates, the Minister for Home Affairs had set out MHA's position concerning the harm reduction approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, we take a harm prevention approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In Singapore, our tough laws have kept the drug situation here relatively under control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we must continue to keep drugs at bay, to prevent the harms from overwhelming us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Countries which adopt harm reduction measures are focused more on minimising further cost from HIV or other blood-borne infections transmitted through intravenous drug use, rather than on preventing drug use, because they have reached a tipping point where drug use is too pervasive to effectively control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: At the same time, as Members have mentioned, we also focus on educating our public on the harms of drugs and adopting evidence-based approaches to rehabilitation and aftercare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Against the backdrop of a worsening global and regional drug situation, we must continue to press on in our fight against drugs, to keep our streets safe and our families protected from the perils of drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: With continued support from Members in the House, our community partners, advocates and members of the public, we will work towards maintaining a drug-free Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I also thank the Minister of State for answering the questions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: For clarity in my speech, when I referred to specific focus on youths, I was actually mooting for greater efforts on the part of MHA to prevent drug abuse amongst youths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I do have one clarification for the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Most of our PDE efforts for youths, are in our schools and the Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: But we need resources for parents to cope as well, especially with new drugs and NPS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Would MHA continue to work with Ministries and other independent bodies to help parents cope with these new drugs and new challenges that parents may face?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In fact, I think CNB had a publication for parents previously called, "start talking before they start taking"?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: So, maybe those resources can be updated and there can be a sustained effort for parents as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As I have shared in my answer, we have the NCPR platform where we not only look at efforts across agencies and the different community organisations, but we also look at specific areas that we want to focus on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: One of the areas that we are looking at today is also about youths' addiction issues, substance abuse – that is one aspect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The other aspect, CNB as the Member has shared, has its own PDE efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The efforts are not only linked with other organisations, but also look at the different segments of the society – parents, students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: At the last MHA COS, I shared that the schools are committed to play a more active role in this aspect, in working together with CNB.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will try to see how we can enhance that effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Another thing that we do, if you look at CNB's social media platforms, they are very active.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: One is about our operations; whenever we make arrests, all these, we will share.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Recently, Mr Christopher de Souza asked about how we can share further, and I shared that it is something that we will continue to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Just a few days ago, I shared about the harms of cannabis on my social media platform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We plan all these holistically, so that we try our best to reach out to the people whom we engage and how we can reach out further with others that we may not have engaged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, going forward, we are exploring ways to navigate this deeper and expand our outreach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Because at the end of the day, as I have shared, with the global situation, I think the only way to go forward is to continue this journey and get as many partners as possible to be on board this journey and protect as many people as possible, especially in Singapore, from the harms of drugs and at the same time, keep our aspiration high for a drug-free Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: For MOF, I think I will follow up separately, after I have read in more detail what was said.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It was mentioned that during this period, there would be industry consultations and so on, to determine if there has been any legitimate use for this product.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not sure, based on the general definition of psychoactive substance, based on what they have, but eventually the substance after due industry consultation is found to have a legitimate use and, therefore, it is eventually not listed in the First Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I mean, will there be such cases and how would they be dealt with?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We also referred to overseas jurisdictions – the United Kingdom and Australia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: What I want to assure Members is that, we have a robust and very careful analysis system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We work very closely with HTX and HSA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In fact, since we shared about the need for this amendment a few years ago, we have been working very hard on the ground from the operational point of view as well as our capability aspect, to determine how we can detect NPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will have to see how the structure of it and if the psychoactive effect is confirmed, then we will be able to take any action.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In this case, with the new amendment, we will look at the psychoactive effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There are, from the scientific point of view, procedures involved, to test the psychoactive effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is consistent with the amendments that we make.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will be looking at the psychoactive effects of the substance.
